title: From question to answer
summary: The six steps of an analysis, turning a vague request into a sharp question, and answering it with formulas you can check.
objectives: Name the six steps of an analysis: ask, get, clean, analyse, check, tell.
Turn a vague request into a sharp question with a measure, a group, a period and a filter.
Answer a sharp question from an order export with COUNTIFS and SUMIFS.
Check an answer before you share it, and say what it can’t tell you.

slides.h: Analysis means answering a question with data
p: Every analysis, from a two-line reply to a board report, follows the same six steps. Skip one and the answer can’t be trusted.
Most of the time goes on **get** and **clean**, not on the clever part.
Going back a step is normal: cleaning often changes the question.
This course follows the six steps, one module at a time.
In real life: was asked “Is Instagram worth it?” She spent ten minutes sharpening the question and an hour on the data. The formula took two minutes.

terms: a file of records copied out of a system, like a website’s orders

items: the data, and look at it
on a copy, never the original

p: A request like “How is Instagram doing?” can’t be answered. A **sharp question** says exactly what to count, for which group, over which period.
If two people could answer it differently, it isn’t sharp yet.
Ask the person what decision the answer is for: that tells you what to measure.
Write the sharp question at the top of your sheet.
In real life: asked for “footfall numbers”. The sharp question turned out to be “Which weekday has the fewest customers per staff member?”: he was planning the rota.

terms: one that only one answer fits

head: Vague request
Sharp question
rows: What was **delivered revenue per month**, April 2025 to March 2026?
What **share of delivered revenue** came from Instagram in FY 2025-26?
What **percentage of order lines** were returned, by category, last quarter?
Which **20% of customers** brought in the most delivered revenue this year?

slides.h: Four parts of a sharp question
p: Most business questions have the same four parts. Name each one and the formula almost writes itself.
**Measure:** revenue, orders, units, customers, a rate.
**Group** and **filter** become the conditions in COUNTIFS and SUMIFS.
**Period:** say the dates. “This year” means different things to finance (April–March) and to everyone else.
In real life: and the sales team argued for a week about “this year’s growth”. Finance meant April–March; sales meant January–December. Same data, two answers.

terms: the number you add, count or average
which rows count, and which don’t

parts: the measure: what to add or count

check.q: Which is the sharpest version of “How are returns?”
options: What percentage of order lines were returned in each category, April–June 2025?
check.explain: It names the measure (percentage returned), the group (category) and the period (April–June 2025).

why.0: Still vague: looking at what, over when?
why.1: “Too high” compared with what? No measure or period.
why.3: That’s a request for data, not a question.

slides.h: Each part of the question becomes part of the formula
p: Once the question is sharp, the formula follows it word for word: the measure is what you add, and the group and filter are the conditions.
The period is the date range of the export; add date conditions when you need a part of it.
Count rows with COUNTIFS, add money with SUMIFS: both from C2.
A share is a part divided by its whole: Instagram ÷ all delivered revenue.
In real life: turned “Is Instagram worth it?” into one SUMIFS. Instagram brought ₹48,610 of ₹2,83,028 delivered revenue in her sample: about 17%.

p: A formula always gives an answer, right or wrong. Before you share it, check it at least two ways.
The quickest check: select the column and read **Sum** and **Count** in the status bar.
If the parts don’t add up, a category is spelt two ways or a row is blank.
Write the check into the sheet as a TRUE/FALSE cell, so it re-checks itself.
In real life: found her “total loans by branch” was ₹2 crore short of the ledger. One branch was spelt “Chennai-T.Nagar” in some rows and “T Nagar” in others.

slides.h: Tell the answer with its limits
p: A good answer gives the number, what it means, and what it **doesn’t** show. That last part stops people drawing the wrong conclusion.
Say the period and any rows you left out.
Separate what the data shows from what you think it means.
Module 7 comes back to honest conclusions with statistics.
In real life: reported “signups doubled” without saying the form had changed to need fewer fields. The board planned for growth that wasn’t real.

terms: a limit on what an answer can show

bad.title: Just the number
bad.text: “Instagram is 17%.” 17% of what? Over when? Is that good?

good.title: The number, the meaning, the limit
good.text: “Instagram brought 17% of delivered revenue in FY 2025-26. This is revenue only: it doesn’t include what we spent on Instagram ads, so it can’t say whether Instagram is profitable.”

check.q: Delivered, returned and cancelled revenue add up to ₹3,10,000, but the Amount column totals ₹3,21,435. What does that suggest?
options: Some rows have a status that isn’t one of the three, like a misspelling or a blank
check.explain: When the parts don’t add up to the whole, some rows fall outside your conditions. Look for spellings and blanks in the Status column.

why.0: SUM adds every number; it doesn’t miss rows.
why.2: Cancelled is one of the three parts you added.
why.3: A gap of ₹11,435 is real money: find it before you report.

demo.intro: Answer “Is Instagram worth it?” as a sharp question: Instagram’s share of delivered revenue, then check that the statuses add up.

cells.N6: Statuses add up to the total?

steps.say: The export: 240 order lines, one product per row. Amount is in column K, Channel in F and Status in L.
How many order lines came through Instagram? COUNTIF on the Channel column.
All delivered revenue: add Amount where Status is Delivered.
Instagram’s delivered revenue: the same, with Channel as a second condition.
Its share: the part divided by the whole.
Check: do the three statuses add up to the whole column? TRUE means nothing fell through the gaps.

demo.outro: A sharp question, one SUMIFS per part, and a check cell that proves the parts add up.

lab.intro: Taraloom’s order export has 240 order lines from the financial year April 2025 to March 2026. Answer the questions in **N2:N6**, putting each answer in column **O**.

cells.N6: Statuses add up to the total?

tasks.prompt: Meera asks “Is Instagram worth it?”. Which is the best sharp question to answer from this export?
hints: It must have a measure, a group and a period.
It must be answerable from the columns you have.
Ad spend isn’t in this export.
tasks.explain: It has a measure (share of delivered revenue), a group (Instagram) and a period, and the export can answer it. Profit needs costs the export doesn’t have.
options: What share of delivered revenue came from Instagram in FY 2025-26?
How much profit did Instagram make?
Show me all the Instagram orders

tasks.prompt: In **O2**, count the order lines that came through **Instagram**.
In **O3**, add up the **Amount** of every **Delivered** order line.
hints: Amount is column K; Status is column L.

mistakes.msg: That adds every status. Add a condition so only Delivered rows count.

tasks.prompt: In **O4**, add up the Amount of order lines that are **Instagram** and **Delivered**.
hints: SUMIFS takes pairs of condition range and condition.

tasks.prompt: In **O5**, show Instagram’s **share** of delivered revenue.
hints: The part is in O4, the whole in O3.

mistakes.msg: Divide the part by the whole: Instagram (O4) ÷ all delivered revenue (O3).

tasks.prompt: In **O6**, check your work: show **TRUE** if delivered (O3) + returned + cancelled revenue equals the total of the whole Amount column.
hints: Work out returned and cancelled with SUMIFS, like O3.
Compare the sum of the three parts with SUM(K2:K241) using =.

expect.regexMsg: Compare the three parts with the total of the whole column, SUM(K2:K241).

tasks.prompt: Which caveat belongs with your answer in O5?
hints: “Worth it” compares what you earn with what you spend.
tasks.explain: The export answers “how much revenue”, not “is it worth it”. Say what the number can’t show.
options: None: the number speaks for itself
It’s revenue only, without Instagram ad costs, so it can’t show whether Instagram is profitable
The sample is too small to calculate a share
Instagram should be compared with TV

quiz.q: Put these first: which step comes before cleaning?
options: Get the data and look at it
quiz.explain: Ask, get, clean, analyse, check, tell.

quiz.q: Which part of “units sold by city in March, excluding returns” is the filter?
quiz.explain: The filter decides which rows count. “By city” is the group and “in March” the period.

quiz.q: Finance says “this year”. In India that usually means…
quiz.explain: The Indian financial year runs from 1 April to 31 March. Always write the dates.

quiz.q: O3 is delivered revenue and O4 is Instagram’s delivered revenue. Which gives Instagram’s share?
Your parts add up to less than the total. What do you look for first?
options: Category values spelt differently, or blanks
quiz.explain: Rows that don’t match any condition fall through the gaps.

options: “Instagram brought 17% of delivered revenue in FY 2025-26; ad costs aren’t included, so this doesn’t show profit.”
quiz.explain: The number, its meaning, and its limit.

points: Six steps: **ask, get, clean, analyse, check, tell**.
A sharp question names a **measure, group, period and filter**; they become your SUMIFS.
Check that the parts add up, then tell the answer **with its limits**.
recap.cheat: Sharp question → one formula per part → a check cell → the answer with its limits.
